Scanning errors read as evident (e.g. qnia, suut, cnm, Cupi = Cum, fum = furor, osse = esse). 1.2.1a: 'decimare' makes no sense; read as 'declinare' or similar ('pass down'). 1.2.5: the text reads 'Balaam'; Bilhah (Bala) is meant. 1.2.10: 'instituamus' rendered as 'intelligamus' (understand); the sentence 'Cubile patris ejus gentes, et corpus dominicum intelligit' is awkward and may be corrupt. 1.3.1a: 'sub ornata pace' probably for 'simulata' or similar; rendered 'feigned'. 1.3.2: 'et gloriari' probably for 'etiam'. 1.3.3: 'a longa terra' read as 'a longe'; the final clause ('excocti lapides … firmitas') is grammatically corrupt. Scripture references as printed are partly off: Ps. 27 (= 28 Hebrew), Prov. 23:4 printed for 18:4, Matt. 20:21, 24 printed for 20:22–23, Gen. 39 printed for 29.

Section 7: 'lime opere' read as 'jam in opere' (fulfilling in deed). Section 2: the Matthew reference 'xxxiii, 18' read as 28:18. Section 5: 'fuerim' read as 'fuerint'. 'Verba dierum' (Words of the Days) is the Hebrew title of Chronicles. In section 8 'Oriens' is rendered 'the Dawn' (often 'the East/Branch'). In section 10, Ps. 58:12 follows the Vulgate wording ('Deus ostendet mihi super inimicos meos'); 'demonstravit' is translated as given.

Scanning errors read as evident: 'vilem' as vitem, 'dius sonis' as divisionis, 'vicium' as victum, 'libum' as cibum, 'regalem' as requiem (the lemma), '[ortis' as fortis, 'tribulis' as tributis, 'Ric' as Hic. 4.8: the citation Rom. iii, 10 should be Rom. 3:20. 4.9: the quotation is from Paul's speech in Acts 13:38-39, though the text attributes it to Peter. 4.6: 'in usus habuisse' rendered 'made use of'. 5.2: 'latratu' (barking, baying) continues the hunting image of Sidon.

7.2: 'Retrorsum enim cadere, esi et hic et inverecunde, tibi non videas, ruere' is corrupt; translated as if 'est et hic inverecunde, ubi non videas, ruere'. 8.2: 'sursum accingentur' ('girded upwards') where the lemma has 'retrorsum'; kept as printed. 'redidiva' read as 'rediviva', 'cis' as 'eis', 'Pharisae' as 'Pharisaeae'. Scripture references corrected where misprinted (Gen. xxviii, 23 and xxxviii, 11 for 37:23 and 37:11).

11.5: 'in (orti' read as 'in forti'. The clause 'tempora futura sterilitate feriret' (struck future times with barrenness) is odd; perhaps it alludes to Joseph's foretelling of the famine. 11.14: 'intra matris ubera' (within the mother's breasts) for catechumens may be an error for 'uterum' (womb), which the contrast with 'those already born' suggests. 'in femorum' read as 'infernorum'. 11.15: 'mutaverunt nomen' is probably for 'mutuaverunt' (borrowed); rendered 'have taken'. 11.13: Mark 15:31 and John 16:26 references in the edition should be 15:34 and 16:28. 11.16: the edition's 'ta capite' is read as 'in capite'.

nodes.text: III. A SHORT BOOK ON THE BLESSINGS OF THE PATRIARCHS.
PREFACE.

The most holy and prophetic blessing of the holy Patriarchs, which was distributed to each in a fitting manner through the Holy Spirit and the mouth of blessed Jacob, cannot be understood in every respect in the literal sense, especially since the same blessed Patriarch says: That I may announce to you the things that are to come in the last days (Gen. 49:1). Nor should it be so thinned out by the allegorical sense that the historical sense must be emptied altogether: for certain things, as we shall see later, were foretold to them in such a way that some came to pass soon, some much later; yet more of them are kept for the end. So let us first, with the Lord's gift, briefly set out what we can understand historically in the words themselves, as though laying foundations; but what wholly escapes the letter, let us examine through spiritual understanding, as things that must be grasped as they were understood, spiritually.
CHAPTER ONE.
The Blessing of Reuben.

1. Reuben, my firstborn; you are my strength and the beginning of my sorrow: first in gifts, greater in rule (ibid., 3). The literal sense is clear, since blessed Jacob received Reuben as his first son by his wife Leah (Gen. 29:31–32); and if he had conducted himself in a way worthy of so great a father, the birthright and the kingship would have belonged to him. Hence he calls him firstborn, as one to whom the gifts of the firstborn were due. He also names him his strength, because the might of rule ought to have passed down to him. But he did not utter these things as statements because he either foresaw or wished that they would be so; rather, to urge him by these words to repentance, when he recalled from how great a dignity he had fallen by sinning.

2. Hence he says: and the beginning of my sorrow. For he was the beginning of his sorrow, who, breaking the reins of chastity, rushed unbridled to defile his father's wife (Gen. 35:22); and this must be believed to have stung him with no small sorrow. And he is rightly called the beginning of sorrow, because the other brothers too were accused by blessed Joseph before their father of a most wicked crime (Gen. 37:2).

3. When he says: first in gifts, it refers to the birthright, which was owed to him as the firstborn. And when he adds: greater in rule, it is openly declared that it had belonged to him that from his seed kings over the other brothers should be raised up.

4. When he says: poured out like water, it has this sense: as water not held in by a vessel flows in every direction, and where a sloping place offers itself lower, falls with its whole force, so you restrained your lust by no marital measure, but wherever the impulse of pleasure enticed you, there you poured out the bilge of your desire. And when he adds: may you not increase, he forbids him from such and similar shamefulness any further. Hence the Lord also [said] to Cain: You have sinned? Be still.

5. What these words aim at, we attest by the words that follow: Because you went up to your father's bed and defiled his couch (Gen. 49:4). For by these words the crime of incest which he had committed with Bilhah, his father's concubine (Gen. 35:22), is plainly magnified. And lest this should perhaps seem forced to anyone, because it was said beforehand: I will announce to you the things that are to come in the last days, let him hear what the book of Chronicles says on this matter: The sons also of Reuben, the firstborn of Israel: for he was indeed his firstborn; but since he had violated his father's bed, his birthright was given to the sons of Joseph, the son of Israel, and he was not reckoned as firstborn (1 Chron. 5:1).

6. Figuratively, however, this firstborn Reuben signifies the Jewish people, who was God's firstborn, according to what the Lord said of him to Moses: Israel is my firstborn son (Exod. 4:22); and blessed Jeremiah: Israel is holy to the Lord, the firstfruits of his harvest (Jer. 2:3). He was his strength when, in the Patriarchs and Prophets and all the other bravest men, he fought bravely against idolatry and the impure throng of all the vices.

7. Yet he afterwards became the beginning of his sorrow, when, at the Saviour's coming, remaining in unbelief, he refused with a swollen mind to accept his teaching. Hence the Lord, seeing the city of Jerusalem, is said to have wept (Luke 19:41), and at the raising of Lazarus he is reported to have shed tears for the blindness of that people (John 11:38).

8. And when he is called first in gifts, it is shown that this people indeed went before in the gifts bestowed by God, but that the Church of the nations would follow, which was to be endowed with the same and far greater gifts of grace. And when it is added: greater in rule, it is no wonder if that nation is honoured which first believed, by the prerogative of the fathers, since the blessed apostle Paul says that the Jew has much advantage in every way (Rom. 3:1–2).

9. Meanwhile he added: You are poured out like water, considering in his mind the unbridledness of that people, which was by no means held in by the vessel of the law and the measure of the divine commandments; but, casting off the bonds of all God's commandments, it poured out the streams of its speech with all its effort toward the Saviour's death. For that speech, good or bad, is signified by water, divine Scripture is witness, which says in a good sense: The words from a man's mouth are deep water (Prov. 18:4); and likewise in a bad sense: He who lets out water is the source of quarrels (Prov. 17:14). And when he adds: may you not increase, he shows that this people, as we also see with our eyes, is reduced to a very small number among all the nations.

10. Why he suffered these things, the following words testify: Because you went up to your father's bed and defiled his couch. By the father's bed let us understand the flesh of the Saviour. Nor is it surprising. By his father's bed he understands the nations and the Lord's body, because that same people was created by him: for it is written of him: All things were made through him (John 1:3). And by the couch the same body is understood, which was, as it were, defiled by the Jews, when at their outcry the Lord was both hung on the cross and pierced with a lance, and drenched with his own blood.
CHAPTER II.
The Blessing of Simeon and Levi.

1. Simeon and Levi are brothers, warring vessels of iniquity (Gen. 49:5). The literal sense is clear: for these two brothers, to avenge the rape of their sister, deceived Shechem and Hamor his father under a feigned peace and false friendship (Gen. 34). He calls them warring vessels of iniquity, because it was very wicked to have offered friendship and afterwards to have betrayed it.

2. Let my soul not come into their counsel (Gen. 49:6); that is, cursing all pretended peace. Hence blessed David too calls down curses on all such deceivers: Who speak peace with their neighbour, but evils are in their filth. Give to them according to their works (Ps. 27:3–4). And when he adds: And in their assembly let my glory not be, he certainly did not wish to glory in such a victory, in which not the courage of the warrior could be praised, but rather the falsehood of the deceiver be convicted.

3. For in their fury they killed a man, and in their self-will they undermined a wall. By the man Shechem should be understood, and through him all who were slain on his account. The undermining of a wall, however, is not read in the book of Genesis to have been carried out there; but this is drawn from the custom of warriors, who, digging the ground from far off by tunnels, usually destroy the foundations of walls and set fire [there], so that, the stones being baked, the firmness and stability of the walls may be thrown down.

4. Let us see with how great a censure he strikes this deed. Cursed, he says, be their fury, because it was stubborn; and their wrath, because it was harsh. For their fury proved stubborn, because it could neither be soothed by blandishments nor softened by gifts. And the wrath was proved harsh, which could not be softened even by the killing of those who had committed the outrage, but rather did not hesitate to rage over the whole city.

5. When he says: I will divide them in Jacob and scatter them in Israel, it properly refers to Levi, which was scattered through all Israel, receiving no inheritance of its own, but, by dwelling in cities and their suburbs, was, as is said here, scattered and divided. For it is the custom of sacred Scripture, when it speaks of those close to it, to foretell in general terms things that usually happen not to all but to some. Hence the Lord too [said] to James and John: Can you drink the cup which I am to drink? You shall indeed drink my cup, he says (Matt. 20:22–23). Yet John did not drink the cup of the passion by shedding his blood.

6. As far as it concerns the prophecy of things to come, by Simeon and Levi the scribes and Pharisees are signified: for it is clear that the chief priests came from Levi. They were the warring vessels of iniquity, having a heart, according to the Lord's reproach, full of iniquity and plunder (Luke 11:39). They warred against the Lord, however, not with a battle of arms but with crafty cunning, seeking how they might overthrow the truthful words and deeds of the Lord with false arguments.

7. Detesting these things, the holy man says: Let my soul not come into their counsel; that is, cursing that counsel which the Jews, gathering together, held, saying: What are we doing, for this man does many signs (John 11:47)? and the rest. And he did not wish his glory to be in their assembly; that is, not wishing to glory in the multitude of those who, the more numerous they were, the worse they were: already fulfilling in deed the sense of the Scripture which says: Do not glory in wicked sons, if they are multiplied (Ecclus. 16:1).

8. He gives the reason why he abhors the counsel and assembly of such men, saying: For in their fury they killed a man, and in their self-will they undermined a wall. For in their fury they killed the Man, that is, the Lord Saviour, of whom Zechariah says: Behold a man: the Dawn is his name (Zech. 6:12), crying out to Pilate: Away with him, away with him, crucify him (John 19:15). And in their self-will they undermined a wall, because, fulfilling their own will, they both crucified the Lord and pierced his side. He is rightly called our wall, because by his protection we are guarded from the hostilities of spiritual enemies. Concerning him it is promised to holy Church in these words: The city of our strength is Zion, the Saviour; a wall and a rampart shall be set in it (Isa. 26:1).

9. This deed the holy man pierces with the sharpest point of a curse, saying: Cursed be their fury, because it was stubborn; and their wrath, because it was harsh. For they had stubborn fury and harsh wrath, because they could neither be brought by divine miracles to believe him God, nor did they spare him, even as an innocent man who did them no harm, but pursued him to the death.

10. What he adds: I will divide them in Jacob and scatter them in Israel, is what we now see. That same people, disinherited of their ancestral soil, pays among all nations the penalty of its faithlessness, as a witness to our belief. This blessed David too prophesied in a psalm in the person of our Lord, saying: My God has shown me [his will] concerning my enemies: do not kill them, lest at any time they forget your law; scatter them by your power (Ps. 58:12). And they are well said to be divided in Jacob and scattered in Israel; because holy Church, which is the supplanter of vices, is rightly called Jacob; and, since it strives to see God by purity of mind, it is called by the name of Israel; through it the Jews wander divided and scattered; and it, spread through the four quarters of heaven, daily bears with them as wanderers.
CHAPTER III.
The Blessing of Judah.

1. Judah, your brothers shall praise you: your hands [shall be] on the necks of your enemies. The sons of your father shall bow down to you (Gen. 49:8). By these words, according to the letter, both the modesty of this man and his abundance of strength are shown: for in dealing courteously with his brothers he appeared of such modesty that he was held worthy of praise by all, which is difficult, namely to have the minds of all reconciled among so many brothers. But he also so abounded in strength that he was able to bend the necks of his enemies. That he was very powerful in eloquence is attested by the speech with which he pleaded his own and his family's need before Joseph (Gen. 42, 43 and 44). Moreover, Josephus the historian relates that he was very powerful with words. Further, that he was held outstanding in strength among his brothers is attested by the Words of the Days, which report it thus: Moreover Judah, who was the strongest among his brothers, from his stock princes sprang (1 Chron. 5:2). What he adds: The sons of your father shall bow down to you, openly entrusts to Judah the kingship which he had taken from Reuben, saying that he was to be bowed down to by his other brothers: which certainly befits royal dignity.

2. Mystically, however, by Judah was even then prefigured he who was born of his stock according to the flesh, our Lord and Saviour; whom all his brothers praise, that is, those who believe in him: hence he himself first, among those who believed in him, sent a command from the tomb through the women, saying: Go and tell my brothers (Matt. 28:10). Lest we think this dignity, of being called his brothers, was granted to the apostles alone, he himself testifies that all who believe in him are to be given this dignity, saying: Whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven, he is my brother, sister and mother (Matt. 12:50). Him therefore his brothers praise; that is, the whole Church, both that which is still exiled on earth from the heavenly inheritance and that which has already gone before to heaven. Hence the psalm: Let heaven and earth praise him (Ps. 68:35). And John in the Apocalypse: Speak praise to our God, all his servants, and you who fear him, small and great (Rev. 19:5). His hands are on the necks of his enemies; because, according to the testimony of the Gospel: The Father gave all things into his hands (John 13:3). He himself also agrees with these words, saying: All power has been given to me in heaven and on earth (Matt. 28:18). And the Father speaks to him: Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet (Ps. 109:1; Matt. 22:44; Luke 20:43). The sons of his father bow down to him; that is, all who through him are adopted into the dignity of sons, as the Apostle says: That at the name of Jesus every knee should bend, of things in heaven, on earth and under the earth.

3. There follows: Judah is a lion's whelp: to the prey, my son, you have gone up: resting you have lain down like a lion, and like a lioness: who shall rouse him? As far as concerns the surface of the letter, the strength of the kings descending from the stock of Judah is prefigured by these words: such as we read blessed David to have been, and blessed Hezekiah, and all the others who, serving the Godhead most humbly, by his gift subdued the forces of their enemies like a lion and a lioness, and were such a terror to their enemies that no one dared to provoke them to battle even when they were at rest: of which the books of Kings are witnesses.

4. Typologically, however, he calls the Lord Saviour a lion's whelp, as sprung from a lion's lineage, that is, begotten of royal stock. And he is well called a lion's whelp, whose nature is said to be that, when born, it sleeps for three days, then, roused by its father's roar, gets up. This figure fits most beautifully the Lord's sleep, in which, sleeping for three days, he cries to the Father: But you, Lord, have mercy on me and raise me up (Ps. 40:11). But, raised up, he went up to the prey; because, despoiling hell, he carried all the just with him to the heights in triumph, as a splendid prey. He lay down like a lion, and as it were like a lioness; because he who willed to sleep in the flesh in the tomb triumphed over his enemies like a victorious lion. What he adds: Who shall rouse him? — understand: but the Father? For no one, I will not say of perishable men, but not even any of the angels, [could], except him of whom the apostle Peter said to the Jews: Whom God raised from the dead, of which we are witnesses (Acts 3:15).

5. The sceptre shall not be taken away from Judah, nor a leader from his thighs, until he comes who is to be sent: and he shall be the expectation of the nations (Gen. 49:10). This saying is understood by the faithful more clearly than light, because that people was ruled by princes and leaders of its own nation for as long as it took for our Lord and Saviour to come, who was to be sent by the Father. He is the expectation of the nations; because, that is, God the Father waited for the nations to repent until, through the coming of his Son, he should call them back from the worship of idolatry to the knowledge of himself. For whether the Jews had been carried off to Babylon, they always had rulers over them from their own nation; or returned from Babylon, until Herod, a foreigner, was set up as their king: and their state was governed by the high priests until it came to Aristobulus, who, first after the return from Babylon, though he was high priest, put a diadem on himself and declared himself king. And likewise his successors, until, as Jewish affairs collapsed, and Hyrcanus, the last king of the Jews, was given over to the utmost evils, Herod the foreigner received the Jewish kingdom from Caesar Augustus. In his time, according to this prophecy and the testimony of the Gospel, he who was to be sent (Matt. 2:1), our Lord and Saviour, came.

6. Binding his foal to the vineyard, and his she-ass, O my son, to the vine (Gen. 49:11). By this arrangement of words it is shown that blessed Jacob is speaking not to Judah, but certainly about him who was to be sent; for one who, speaking to a son, says O my son, and adds your foal or your she-ass, is most plainly speaking about him whom he had foretold above was to be sent: whom we read (Matt. 21:5-7), coming into Jerusalem, made use of a she-ass and a foal, and yet they were not tied to a vineyard or a vine. It remains, then, that nothing historical be sought in these words, but that the whole be understood as said typologically. For the Lord and Saviour bound his foal to the vineyard when he subjected the untamed people of the nations to the precepts of the apostles, who were begotten from the Jewish vineyard, of which Isaiah [says]: For the vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel (Isa. 5:7). He also tied his she-ass, that is, the Synagogue, to the vine, that is, the Church; calling her back from unbelief at the end of the age, he will subject her, weighed down by the yoke of the law, to discipleship of the Church, and so there will be one flock and one shepherd (John 10:16); and according to the testimony of blessed Zechariah, those two rods will be joined, and will be in union in the hand of the Lord.

7. He will wash his robe in wine, and his cloak in the blood of the grape (Gen. 49:11). It is agreed to be an idiom of Hebrew speech to repeat one and the same thing in different words, as here. For what is wine but the blood of the grape? But as much as the surface of the letter is incoherent (for no one washes either a robe or a cloak in wine), so much the more is it commended inwardly by a more pleasing understanding. For the Saviour washed his robe in wine and his cloak in the blood of the grape, because, hanging on the cross, he willed that his sacred flesh, which was his robe, be drenched in his own blood.

8. There follows: His eyes are more beautiful than wine, and his teeth whiter than milk (ibid., 12). The eyes of the Saviour are proclaimed more beautiful than wine, because the gifts of the Holy Spirit, which are conferred through Christ, are shown to be lovelier than the wine of the law. For that the eyes of the Saviour signify the gifts of the Holy Spirit, the prophet Zechariah testifies, saying: Upon one stone are seven eyes (Zech. 3:9); which Isaiah enumerates, saying: The spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of knowledge and piety, and the spirit of the fear of the Lord (Isa. 11:2-3). These are more beautiful than the wine of the law which failed at the wedding (John 2:3), because through the law [comes] knowledge of sin (Rom. 3:20), but through the grace of the Holy Spirit its remission is granted to us. And according to the Gospel, the law was given through Moses, but grace and truth through Jesus Christ (John 1:17).

9. As for what is said: And his teeth whiter than milk: by the teeth the preachers of the New Testament should be understood, who, by breaking up spiritual foods, that is, by expounding them, pass on to us many very useful things into the belly of memory. Milk, moreover, is not unfittingly taken as the teaching of the Old Testament, which was laid down for a people just beginning and still too weak for solid food. Jesus therefore has teeth whiter than milk, because he has made the preachers of his Church conspicuous for the cleanness of purity. For how far the followers of the Gospel differ from the observances of the law, blessed Peter is witness, who says: You could not be justified in the law: in him everyone who believes is justified (Acts 13:38-39). These teeth, then, are white, because, washed in the font of baptism, they are made most pure of the blemishes of sins. Of the observers of the law, however, nothing of the kind is reported, but it is only said that He who does these things shall live in them (Gal. 3:12). Moreover, all who serve the law carnally are under a curse, since the same Law says terribly: Cursed is everyone who does not abide in the commandments of this law, to do the things that are written in it (Deut. 27:26).
CHAPTER IV.
The Blessing of Zebulun.

1. Zebulun shall dwell on the shore of the sea, and in the harbour of ships, reaching as far as Sidon (Gen. 49:13). According to the history, [this] is foretold of the portion which he was to receive by God's gift in the land of promise: namely, that the land of his possession would begin at the sea on one side and end at a torrent on the other, as is plainly declared in the book of Joshua son of Nun (Josh. 19:11), where the allotments of their possessions are defined: hence Sidon too is mentioned here, which lies next to the sea.

2. According to the mystical senses, however, Zebulun designates the firstfruits of the holy Church; some of the holy apostles are believed to have been of his tribe, because they lived constantly on the seashore, since, getting their living from it by hand and skill, they were called by the Lord to the summit of the apostolate, according to the prophecy of blessed David, who says: The princes of Judah their leaders, the princes of Zebulun, the princes of Naphtali (Ps. 67:28). They also dwell in the harbour of ships, because they rest confidently in secure peace in the Lord Jesus Christ. For the ships are understood as the churches, which in the most trustworthy harbour seek the Lord, the port of their salvation, and find him. And it is well added: Reaching as far as Sidon; because, that is, the same holy Church is not confined to one corner of the world, but by growing has come to the peoples of the gentiles. For Sidon is interpreted 'hunting', signifying, as has been said, the gentile world, which with bestial ways pursued the worship of idolatry like the lairs of the wilderness. It afterwards deserved, by the net of the Lord's preaching and the baying of the holy apostles, to be admitted within the enclosures of the holy Church.
CHAPTER V.
The Blessing of Issachar.

1. Issachar, a strong ass lying down between the boundaries. He saw that rest was good, and the land that it was excellent, and he put his shoulder under to carry, and became a servant under tribute (Gen. 49:14-15). By these words this tribe is signified as one that would devote itself to the teaching of the law, and would apply itself more readily to searching out the commandments of God. For it is said to have seen that rest was good, and the land that it was excellent; that is, to have tasted in mind how sweet it was to occupy one's understanding with God's commandments. And therefore it is said to have put its shoulder under to carry, that is, to have turned its mind with all its effort to searching out the utterances of the divine word: and for this reason all those beneath it brought it gifts and honour as to a master and teacher. The book of Chronicles agrees with this understanding, which says of this tribe: Of the sons of Issachar also, learned men, who knew each of the times, to direct what the princes ought to do (1 Chron. 12:32).

2. This strong ass, moreover, bears the type of the gentile people, which before it had the Lord as its rider was brutish, and, impatient of bridles, was carried along at its own whim. But after it deserved to have the Lord as rider, it borrowed from him the name of strong ass. It saw that rest was good, hearing from its rider: Come to me, all you who labour and are burdened, and I will give you rest (Matt. 11:28). And it looked out on the land, that it was excellent; because, leaving the empty teachings of the philosophers, it turned most zealously to the reading of sacred Scripture. Hence, because it learned among other things that not the hearers of the law are justified (Rom. 2:13), it is added: he put his shoulder under to carry; that is, it subjected all its strength to the divine commandments, and above all in the love of God and of neighbour. For a neighbour is not loved unless he is carried. And it is added: and became a servant under tribute; for it pays as it were a kind of tribute daily, hearing from the Apostle: Render to all their dues: fear to whom fear, honour to whom honour, tax to whom tax (Rom. 13:7), and the rest.
CHAPTER VI.
The Blessing of Dan.

1. Dan shall judge his people, like another tribe in Israel. Let Dan be a snake in the way, a horned serpent in the path, biting the hooves of the horse, so that its rider falls backward. I will wait for your salvation, Lord (Gen. 49:16-18). Historically, indeed, it is foretold that not only from the other, nobler tribes but also from Dan a prince would come for Israel, and by way of description what kind he would be is indicated. For Samson is prefigured by these words, who was terrible after the manner of a snake and serpent: and to suggest him as more terrible, he is described as horned, because of his exceptional power and strength. He therefore beset the ways and paths of the Israelite kingdom in the time of his rule, so that none of the enemies should dare to invade the land under his authority by force. And if anyone more savage, trusting in his own speed as of a horse and in his strength, had wished to attack him, he would soon, gnawing away the soles of his feet and consuming his strength to stand, throw his pursuer to the ground. Lest anyone, deceived by error, should reckon him more than a man, he at once added who was truly the prince to be awaited, saying: I will wait for your salvation, Lord; of whom, that is, this man went before as a type in some part.

2. This Dan, moreover, prefigures the Antichrist, who will be like a snake in the way and a horned serpent in the path: for to those walking in the way and path of God's commandments he sets himself up as an obstacle, as far as lies in him, armed against them with a twofold cunning. In the serpent his craftiness is prefigured, because he seeks to deceive by guile those who keep the way of the Lord with the step of works. In the horns his fury is shown, which he will use against those whom he could not deceive by crafty scheming. For *cerasta* in Greek are called horns in Latin; and for this reason this serpent is described as horned. So when the Antichrist, on coming, has done great signs before the eyes of the onlookers and brought fire down from on high, he is a serpent in the way (Rev. 13:13). But when he has turned to inflicting punishments and torments on those who do not believe him, he becomes a horned serpent in the path; for he strives to subdue to himself, with the horns of power, those who walk along the narrow path of the Lord. While he exalts himself above all that is called God or that is worshipped (2 Thess. 2:4), he bites the hooves of the horse, so that its rider falls backwards: for he takes away worldly glory from those who do not yield to him, to the end that, enticed by love of present goods, they may fall there where they do not see. For to fall backwards is both to rush headlong shamelessly here, where you do not see, and afterwards to come into the outer darkness. For whoever falls on his face blushes for what he has done in the past; but whoever falls backwards, as we have already said, with an impenitent heart nurses wrath for himself on the day of wrath (Rom. 2:5). Further, lest anyone think the Antichrist should be worshipped as God because of the great loftiness of his miracles, he added: I will wait for your salvation, Lord; as if he were saying: although the Antichrist shines with many marks of miracles, yet for me your Salvation, which in Hebrew is called Jesus, is to be awaited, so that he, coming, may crush this man's power with eternal punishment, and, finding me among his faithful, may grant me a blessed dwelling.
CHAPTER VII.
The Blessing of Gad.

1. Gad, girded, will fight before him, and he himself will be girded backwards (Gen. 49:19). The literal sense is plain to those who read the book of Joshua son of Nun: for Gad, who sought and received from Moses an inheritance across the Jordan, earned possession of it on this condition, that, girded with arms before Israel, with Reuben and the half-tribe of Manasseh joined to him, he should advance fighting against the enemies (Deut. 3:18); and this he afterwards did under Joshua. Yet when the enemies had been subdued, and he returned back to his own possession, he had to withstand the incursions of the neighbouring nations (1 Chron. 5:18). This, then, is what he says: that first he fought girded before his brothers, and afterwards was girded again for battles.

2. Spiritually, however, it signifies all the elect from among the Jews, who stood forth as leaders, as it were, for the new people, and led them into the land once promised. Such were the prophets and the holy patriarchs, who pierced idolatry, the mother of all vices, and its countless offspring with the darts of their words. Yet they will be girded upwards again, for in the last times, when the fullness of the Gentiles enters, they will be roused to renewed contests, which they will have with the Antichrist and his henchmen. For now they do not have an inheritance across the streams of the Jordan, because they do not enter the Church through the grace of Baptism, but dwell apart, outside their brothers, remaining in the ceremonies of the Law.
CHAPTER VIII.
The Blessing of Asher.

1. Asher, his bread is rich, and he will furnish delicacies to kings (Gen. 49:20). According to the letter, abundance of land seems to be promised to this tribe; for in the lot of its possession it had Mount Carmel, notable for its fertility; and at the same time it bordered on the sea, and so there is no doubt that it offered even to its kings the delicacies of sea and land with which it abounded.

2. By these words, however, are foretold the holy men who would come from the Synagogue, whose bread is rich; namely, prophetic teaching overflowing with the fatness of the Holy Spirit. One of them, burning with insatiable eagerness, cried: Let my soul be filled as with fat and richness (Ps. 62:6). They serve their delicacies to kings; for to those who desire to hold a reign of just restraint in themselves and over those subject to them, they show beforehand the royal rule.
CHAPTER IX.
The Blessing of Naphtali.

1. Naphtali, a stag let loose, and giving words of beauty (Gen. 49:21). From the teaching of blessed Jerome we learn that the Hebrew does not have 'a stag let loose' but 'a well-watered field', and that by the well-watered field is signified the abundance of hot waters which well up most plentifully in the outskirts of Tiberias. Yet it is a tradition of the Hebrews that this city was most zealous for the divine commandments; and that therefore the well-watered field signifies the most abundant teaching of the instructing masters, which was wont, like a stream, to drench the hearts of the ignorant so that they brought forth the fruits of understanding; and that this is explained in what follows, when it is said: giving words of beauty.

2. We, however, understand by Naphtali the holy preachers of the Church, who, sent to the holy Church, know how to make leaps of understanding in the manner of stags, and fearlessly to climb the mountains of contemplation, and so to give words of beauty to the peoples: so that what they have learned when raised up to the height of contemplation, they diligently minister to those placed below.
CHAPTER X.
The Blessing of Joseph.

1. A growing son is Joseph, a growing son, and comely in appearance (Gen. 49:22; 39:6). According to the letter, blessed Jacob foresaw that the tribe of Joseph would abound in countless offspring; whence he was also the father of two tribes, as [Jacob] had foretold when blessing them above. Hence, as if blessing two tribes, he repeated: a growing son.

2. It is agreed, moreover, that Joseph went before as a type of the Saviour, because he feeds Egypt, failing with hunger, with the grain of the word of God: and, sold by his brothers the Jews, he nourishes the Church of the Gentiles to this day. To him it is said: a growing son, and comely in appearance; for he, the Son of God and likewise the Son of Man, in a certain manner grew when he took to himself, in the Apostles and the other faithful of that time, the people of Israel, who dishonoured God by transgressing the Law. He is likewise a growing son when he spread the knowledge of his name among the Gentiles too, and grows among them to the end of the world through the enlightenment of faith and works. And the same Joseph is comely in appearance, because he is beautiful in form beyond the sons of men (Ps. 44:3).

3. The daughters ran to and fro upon the wall. But they embittered him, and quarrelled, and envied him, having darts (Gen. 49:22-23). As far as the historical event is concerned, he calls his brothers daughters because of the disgrace of their inhumanity. For it was not the part of manly and steady counsel to have wished either to kill an innocent brother or to sell him, but rather of womanly fickleness. They ran upon the wall, because they thought they had found an unassailable plan concerning him, so that he should not become their king. They embittered him, stripping him of his many-coloured tunic (Gen. 37:23), and subjecting him to undeserved insults. And they quarrelled and envied him, having darts: Shall you be our king? Or shall we be subject to your authority (Gen. 37:8)? Hence it was said above: So his brothers envied him (Gen. 37:11). And they had darts; that is, hearts ready to do harm. Hence of the Jews who desired to kill the Lord it is said: The arrows of little ones have become their wounds (Ps. 63:9).

4. According to the mystical senses, however, the daughters are understood as the Jews, who are reckoned under a feminine name because, abandoning the Lord and the solid teaching of our Saviour and clinging to the superstition of the Pharisees, they were disturbed in mind. For those who lack solid sense, and whose mind wavers with changeable fluctuation, are reckoned by the Apostle under the name of women, when he says of bad teachers: Who make their way into houses and lead captive silly women laden with sins, always learning and never arriving at the knowledge of the truth (2 Tim. 3:6). They ran upon the wall when they thought they had found a most secure plan, as Caiaphas said: It is expedient for you that one man should die for the people, and that the whole nation should not perish (John 11:50). They embittered him when, moved in a certain manner by weariness at their unbelief, he said: O perverse generation, how long shall I be with you? How long shall I bear with you (Mark 9:19)? They quarrelled, saying: How long will you take away our soul (John 10:24)? And they envied him when they said in their council: What shall we do, for this man does many signs? If we let him go on thus, all will believe in him (John 11:47-48). And again: Do you see that we achieve nothing? See, the whole world has gone after him (John 12:19). They had darts, of which it is written: The arrows of little ones have become their wounds (Ps. 63:9).

5. His bow rested on the strong one, and the bonds of his arms and of his hands were loosed by the hands of the mighty one of Jacob: from there the shepherd went forth, the stone of Israel (Gen. 49:24). The historical sense, as far as it is given to be understood, is this. By the bow is understood a mind that foreknows things to come. For an arrow is set on a bow so that it may strike from afar; and a mind that foresees the future is accustomed to send the arrows of its pronouncements a long way. So the saying, his bow rested on the strong one, is as if he said: his mind, afflicted on every side by tribulations, found rest; on the strong one, that is, made firm in God, and by the arrows of its pronouncements, foretelling what was to come, it struck at future times with barrenness.

6. And what he says, And the bonds of his arms and of his hands were loosed, refers to the time when he was released from prison at Pharaoh's command, and, as it is said here, the bonds of his arms and of his hands, with which he had been ordered to be bound in prison, were loosed by the hands, that is, by the power, of the mighty one of Jacob, namely of God almighty, by whose help Jacob shone with might.

7. Further, what he adds, from there the shepherd went forth, the stone of Israel, refers to Christ, who went forth from Jacob, that is, drawing his origin from him. He is rightly called the stone of Israel, because he is strength to the one who believes in him.

8. To the Saviour, moreover, this saying applies in this way. His bow rested on the strong one; that is, the sentence of punishment by which the Jews were to be struck, who refused to receive him but persecuted him even to death, rested on the strong one, that is, was fixed with steadfast unchangeableness together with the Father, as he said: Amen I say to you, there shall not be left here one stone upon another (Matt. 24:2). And: Behold, your house shall be left to you desolate, etc. (Matt. 23:38).

9. And the bonds of his arms and of his hands were loosed by the hands of the mighty one of Jacob, when the bonds of the tomb were untied, and by the hands of the mighty one of Jacob, that is, by the power of the Father, resurrection was not denied him.
10. And from there the shepherd went forth, and the stone of Israel; that is, the Lord and Saviour, going forth from God the Father, presented himself to human sight, as he himself said:
I came forth from the Father, and have come into the world (John 16:28).

11. The God of your father shall be your helper, and the Almighty shall bless you with blessings of heaven above, with blessings of the deep that lies below, with blessings of the breasts and of the womb (Gen. 49:25). He calls down upon his son the help of the God of his father, namely of him by whose help he remembered he had been delivered from such great dangers, and whom he had come to know as almighty through the benefits granted to him. What he says, with blessings of heaven above, concerns rain and the mildness of the air, by which the earth is made fruitful with crops and the produce of trees is nourished. What he adds, with blessings of the deep that lies below, concerns the fertility of the earth, which, like the hollows of a sponge, is watered by the vapours of the deep, so that it is not easily parched by the fires of the sun and made useless by drought. When he blesses with blessings of the breasts and of the womb, [it is] so that he may grow with numerous offspring, and not be condemned to barrenness either of the men or of the women.

12. And he says: The blessings of your father have been strengthened by the blessings of his fathers (ibid., 26); that is, so that Joseph should not doubt that what holy Jacob promised him would come to pass, not so much from his own, as it were new, blessing, but because it had long since been promised to his fathers, that is, Abraham and Isaac. For this is what he says: the blessings of your father have been strengthened, as if he said: do not take these blessings of your father as his own, nor as given once, but [know] that they were first given by God to my fathers, and not once but often. And hence it is that I pour out upon your head, by the Lord's authority, the same blessings that were promised to me and to my fathers.

13. To the Lord and Saviour, moreover, God almighty and the Father was a helper, when he cried in the psalm: Help me, O Lord my God; save me according to your mercy (Ps. 108:26). For he who by undivided Godhead gives aid to all who are proclaimed, being made man and made a little lower than the angels (Heb. 2:7), needed not only the Father's help but also that of an angel, namely so as to show forth the twofold substance in himself. For hence it is that he cries out: God, my God, why have you forsaken me (Mark 15:34)? And in the Gospel: There appeared to him an angel from heaven, strengthening him (Luke 22:43). And the Almighty himself blessed him, saying: This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased (2 Pet. 1:17).

14. He blessed him with blessings of heaven above and with blessings of the deep that lies below when, according to the Apostle, He gave him the name which is above every name, that at his name every knee should bow, of things on earth, in heaven, and below the earth (Phil. 2:10). He exalted him with blessings of the breasts and of the womb when, in the sons of the Church, some catechumens, lying as it were still within the mother's breasts, others, after the manner of those already born, sucking at the mother's breasts, he grants that he be blessed throughout the world. For those who have not yet come out into the strength of faith, but are drawn to it by guides, hear from the Apostle: My little children, with whom I am again in labour until Christ be formed in you (Gal. 4:19). And those who have already received the rudiments of faith, but have not yet fully grown together in firmness of doctrine, hear from the same: I gave you milk to drink, not solid food; for you were not yet able, and even now you are not able (1 Cor. 3:2).

15. There follows: Until the desire of the everlasting hills should come (Gen. 49:26). Here nothing sounds of history, but all of the divine. For he foretells that the people of Israel will be sustained by these blessings until the desire of the everlasting hills should come. For by hills are understood the saints established in the Church, who, although they excel in the merit of their virtues, yet out of most devout humility remember that they are hills. Hence the psalm: Let the mountains receive peace for the people, and the hills justice (Ps. 71:3). For it is agreed that their desire was always the coming of the Lord Jesus. Hence first Moses: I beseech you, Lord, send him whom you will send (Exod. 4:13). And blessed Simeon received an answer from the Holy Spirit that he would not see death until he first saw the Lord's Christ (Luke 2:26). They are called everlasting hills because they are known to have been created by God for eternity. For their purpose is not changed this way and that, as is that of fools; but always tending towards eternity and cleaving to the Eternal, they too have taken from him the name of eternity. For of fools it is said: For the fool changes like the moon (Ecclus. 27:12); but of the truly wise: The wise man abides like the sun (ibid.).

16. There follows: May they be on the head of Joseph, and on the crown of the Nazarite among his brothers (Gen. 49:26). These blessings were on the head of Joseph, because through Christ all praise and blessing is rendered to the Father. Hence he himself says to the Father: Father, glorify your Son, that your Son also may glorify you (John 17:1). And they are rightly said to be on his head, because the head of Christ is God (1 Cor. 11:3). And the son himself is called a Nazarite among his brothers, because he is holy with a special dignity, which is what Nazarite means. Of him Scripture says most truly that he committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth (1 Pet. 2:22); and him God the Father anointed with a special anointing above his fellows (Heb. 1:9).
CHAPTER XI.
The blessing of Benjamin.

1. Benjamin, a ravening wolf, in the morning shall eat the prey, and in the evening shall divide the spoils (Gen. 49:27). The tradition of the Hebrews, with the agreement of blessed Jerome, holds that these words signify the altar of Jerusalem, which is known to have been built in the tribe of Benjamin. Like a ravening wolf it devoured the morning sacrifice by the burning of fire; but in the evening, when the sacrifices and the ceremonies of the victims were completed, it used to divide among the priests and Levites those portions which were left over by the fire and were owed by the command of the Law for the priests' food.

2. Moreover, by this saying is signified blessed Paul, who was to come from the same tribe, who like a ravening wolf ate in the morning, that is, in his youth; since, while consenting to the death of blessed Stephen, and receiving letters from the chief priests and elders of the Jewish people to Damascus and to the other cities, as many saints as he tore with various slaughter, so many prey did he eat, as it were, like a ravening wolf. Yet in the evening he divided the spoils when, laid low by the Lord's voice and vision, he distributed the fitting nourishment of divine doctrine to the faithful established within holy Church: to some, as to little ones in Christ, giving the milk of wisdom; with some, still suffering with them, he grieves like a woman in labour; but to the more perfect handing over the solid food of doctrine. For that spoils signify the divine commandments, David is witness, saying: I will rejoice over your words, as one who finds much spoil (Ps. 118:162). And blessed Isaiah of the Apostles: They shall rejoice before you, as they rejoice in the harvest, as they exult who divide the spoils (Isa. 9:3).
